body.text: Japan-Vietnam relations have entered a new phase. Since the November 2023 upgrade to a “Comprehensive Strategic Partnership for Peace and Prosperity in Asia and the World,” the two governments have steadily expanded cooperation across economic security, the green transition, advanced technology, maritime and security cooperation, and development. The question now is not how much more can be added to the bilateral agenda, but whether the two countries can turn an increasingly ambitious partnership into tangible economic and strategic results.

This evolving relationship reflects two distinct strategic calculations. They are complementary, but not identical. For Japan, Vietnam is becoming increasingly important to economic security, supply chain diversification, and resilience, particularly in energy and critical minerals. In May 2026, the two governments identified economic security as a new priority for bilateral relations, focusing on energy, critical minerals, AI, semiconductors, and space. For Vietnam, the emphasis remains on independence, self-reliance, diversification, and multilateralization in its external relations. The partnership will work best when it expands both countries’ strategic options rather than forcing alignment into an exclusive framework.
Economic Security Without Strategic Polarization

Energy security offers the clearest test of this new phase of partnership amid continued geopolitical uncertainty in the Middle East. Support for the Nghi Son refinery shows how bilateral cooperation can serve both countries’ interests. At their May 2026 summit, Japan and Vietnam agreed to proceed with support from NEXI, Japan’s official export credit agency, for crude oil procurement for Nghi Son. It will be the first project under POWERR Asia, a broader partnership designed to maintain crude oil and petroleum production and key supply chains.

On rare earths and other critical minerals, Japan sees Vietnam as an important partner in diversifying supply chains and reducing dependence on China. But Vietnam remains closely tied to China, which produces over 90 percent of the world’s refined rare earths and almost all high-performance magnets. Vietnam still lacks independent separation and refining capacity. As its electronics and EV industries expand, this dependence may deepen. Against this backdrop, the May summit treated critical minerals cooperation more cautiously, emphasizing continued discussions rather than announcing concrete projects.

For Vietnam, mineral resources alone do not automatically translate into an autonomous supply chain. Developing domestic processing, technological capability, and downstream industries will take time. Economic resilience is not the same as economic decoupling from China. Given these constraints, the most tangible near-term progress will likely come in energy security, while critical minerals cooperation can be expected to advance more gradually and selectively.

Vietnam’s foreign policy centers on independence and self-reliance, coupled with a diversified and multilateral external posture. Japan’s most valuable contribution may therefore be to broaden Vietnam’s economic and technological options rather than frame the relationship as a choice between strategic partners. Japan has relatively little to gain from presenting its engagement as an effort to draw Vietnam away from China. Its greater contribution lies in giving Vietnam a wider range of economic and technological options.
Advanced Technology as the New Growth Engine

Looking further ahead, some of the greatest opportunities lie at the intersection of advanced technology, digitalization, the green transition, semiconductors, and human capital. The challenge is to pursue them as part of a wider economic and industrial ecosystem rather than as separate initiatives.

Some foundations are already in place. Japan and Vietnam are establishing cooperation channels through the Asia Zero Emission Community (AZEC), while the Joint Crediting Mechanism (JCM) provides a bilateral framework for decarbonization technologies and infrastructure. Cooperation is also extending into science and technology, semiconductors, AI, energy, critical minerals, and agriculture. Specific areas include semiconductor R&D and education, AI and human resource development, satellite data, digital transformation, and energy cooperation.

The larger strategic prize is not any single investment but a durable ecosystem connecting skills, research and development, manufacturing, supply chains, and ultimately markets across the two economies. Japan can contribute capital, technology, an established industrial base, and institutional know-how, while Vietnam offers an expanding production base and a growing pool of human resources. A long-term road map, with carefully chosen flagship projects at its heart, could turn these complementary strengths into industrial upgrading and a more substantial economic relationship.
The Implementation Challenge

The challenge is not simply to raise ambition but to create the conditions for that ambition to be realized. Persistent concerns among Japanese businesses make regulatory predictability, administrative efficiency, access to financing, and appropriate risk-sharing essential to the bilateral economic agenda. Japan’s focus at the May 2026 summit on the investment and economic cooperation environment is a clear example. Ultimately, strategic cooperation will be credible only if it produces projects that are economically viable and sustainable without indefinite government support.

The Japan-Vietnam Joint Initiative is a key institutional underpinning. Established in 2003 to support improvements in Vietnam’s investment climate and institutional framework, it reflects Japan’s long-standing commitment to addressing practical impediments to the bilateral relationship. But the context has changed considerably. Vietnam has developed significantly in its capabilities and in the range of partners it can now engage with. History gives Japan credibility in Vietnam, but it does not guarantee future relevance. Japan must demonstrate the specific value a deeper relationship can bring.

Both sides therefore need to further substantiate the partnership. Vietnam can continue working to create a more transparent and predictable investment climate, while Japan can go beyond identifying institutional impediments to put forward a more compelling economic case.

A disciplined approach to risk is just as important. Government support should address risks the market cannot efficiently bear, not shield private investors from ordinary commercial risk. Clear allocation of risk between government and business should be central to public-private collaboration. An arm’s-length relationship upholds the investor’s autonomy and ownership, rather than subordinating their interests to the government’s geopolitical objectives.
An Autonomous Partnership for Regional Stability

The same logic applies to regional and security cooperation. Vietnam has become an increasingly important partner in Japan’s Indo-Pacific diplomacy under the updated Free and Open Indo-Pacific (FOIP). Vietnam’s commitment to strategic autonomy is not an obstacle to deeper cooperation with Japan. It is precisely what makes a non-exclusive partnership politically sustainable.

There is ample scope for deeper cooperation on the maritime order, climate resilience, energy security, and technological resilience in ways that serve both countries’ interests while respecting Vietnam’s diplomatic independence. This aligns with the principles set out in the 2023 Comprehensive Strategic Partnership, particularly international law, sovereignty, independence, peace, and shared prosperity.

The relationship therefore goes well beyond bilateral interests. Japan and Vietnam can show that a meaningful strategic relationship is possible without being exclusive. ASEAN-centric institutions, APEC, and other international fora provide mechanisms through which this can contribute to regional stability and cooperation.

The timing of General Secretary and State President To Lam’s visit from November 8 to November 11 is very deliberate. With a summit coming just before APEC and the ASEAN-related meetings, both countries can highlight their bilateral cooperation within broader regional discussions on supply chains, energy transition, and nontraditional security.

The first phase of the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership was about building the architecture of cooperation. The next is about implementation. Japan’s technology, finance, capacity to develop human capital, and ability to share appropriate risk can be brought together to support Vietnam’s development priorities. At the same time, a more transparent and predictable investment climate in Vietnam will be essential for turning strategic intent into actual projects.

The next phase of Japan-Vietnam relations should therefore be judged less by the number of agreements signed than by whether the partnership produces bankable projects, stronger capabilities, and greater economic resilience. Japan does not need Vietnam to choose between strategic partners, and Vietnam does not need Japan simply to add another diplomatic framework. What both need is a partnership that expands their room for maneuvering while delivering tangible economic value.
Following Lam’s visit to Japan next week, the next test will be whether the two governments can translate another round of high-level diplomacy into tangible results and measurable progress.
